text: iCall — free online therapy India: Run by TISS (Tata Institute of Social Sciences). Completely free. Offers individual counseling via phone (9152987821) and email (icall@tiss.edu). Staffed by trained counselors and psychologists, not just volunteers. Also provides LGBTQ+-affirming counseling and student-specific support. One of the most credible free mental health services in India.

YourDOST — online therapy platform: Offers individual therapy sessions at approximately ₹1,200-3,000 per session depending on therapist seniority. Has a peer support and expert chat feature. Used by many university campuses as embedded student wellness tool. Therapists are verified professionals. Also has a free Q&A forum. Available in Hindi and English.

MindPeers — corporate mental health focus: Primarily serves corporate employees via employer-sponsored programs. Sessions are available at ₹1,500-2,500. If your company has a MindPeers partnership, sessions may be free or subsidized. Offers EAP (Employee Assistance Program) integration. Less accessible for self-paying individuals but strong for working professionals.

Wysa — AI + human therapy app: Wysa offers an AI chatbot for daily mood tracking and CBT-based exercises, plus optional human coaching and therapy sessions. The base app is free. Human therapist sessions are ₹1,800-3,500. Evidence-backed: Wysa has published peer-reviewed research on its efficacy. Good entry point for people not yet ready for live therapy.

Lissun — affordable Hindi-language therapy: Lissun specifically targets Hindi-speaking users who are uncomfortable in English-medium therapy. Offers sessions at ₹500-1,500, making it more accessible than most platforms. Has therapists specializing in relationship issues, trauma, and academic stress. Filling an important gap for non-metro, Hindi-belt users.

Vandrevala Foundation — free helpline and therapy: 1860-2662-345 (24/7 free helpline). Also offers subsidized in-person and online therapy. The foundation operates clinics in several cities. For people who cannot afford private therapy, Vandrevala's foundation arm provides low-cost sessions. One of the few organizations providing both crisis and ongoing therapy at scale.

Intellecte — online therapy India: Offers one-on-one therapy with verified psychologists. Sessions are mid-range priced (₹1,000-2,500). Has a matching system to connect clients with therapists based on presenting concern and language preference. Supports Hindi, English, and some regional languages. Good for people who want a structured therapist-matching process.

InnerHour — app and therapy platform: InnerHour combines self-help tools (mood tracker, journaling, guided exercises) with professional therapy. Therapy sessions range from ₹1,200-2,500. The app is free and has programs for anxiety, depression, sleep, and stress. Recommended as a step-up from pure self-help before full therapy.

Government NMHP resources — district mental health programs: Under India's National Mental Health Programme, every district is supposed to have a District Mental Health Programme (DMHP) providing free outpatient psychiatric care. Services include free medications, therapy (where available), and referrals. Access point is usually the district government hospital. Quality varies by state — Maharashtra, Kerala, and Karnataka tend to have stronger programs.

Tele-MANAS — national government tele-mental health: Launched in 2022, Tele-MANAS (14416 or 1-800-891-4416 toll-free) connects callers to trained counselors and psychiatrists across India. Available in 20+ languages. Free. Designed specifically to scale mental health access to rural and underserved populations. Linked to NIMHANS and AIIMS tele-psychiatry networks.

LGBTQ+ affirming resource — Humsafar Trust Mumbai: Mumbai-based NGO providing mental health, legal, and community support for LGBTQ+ individuals. Has a counseling center and regular support groups. Offers counseling by LGBTQ+-affirming therapists trained in queer-affirmative therapy. Contact: 022-26673800. Also runs a helpline for LGBTQ+ crisis and general support.

LGBTQ+ affirming resource — iCall: iCall (9152987821) specifically trains its counselors in LGBTQ+-affirmative practice. Has published guidelines on queer-affirmative therapy. Callers can disclose their sexual orientation or gender identity without fear of judgment or conversion-oriented responses. One of the safest helpline options for LGBTQ+ individuals in India.

LGBTQ+ affirming resource — Nazariya Delhi: Delhi-based queer feminist organization providing mental health support, advocacy, and community space for LGBTQ+ individuals — with a specific focus on queer women, trans, and non-binary people. Offers counseling and group support. Contact via their website or Facebook page for current helpline access.

LGBTQ+ affirming resource — Sappho Kolkata: Sappho for Equality is Kolkata-based and provides support for lesbian, bisexual, and transgender individuals in Eastern India. Has a helpline (033-24740042) and offers counseling, legal aid, and community support. Important resource for LGBTQ+ individuals in Bengal and Northeast India.

LGBTQ+ affirming resource — Sahodaran Chennai: Chennai-based organization supporting gay, bisexual, and transgender men in South India. Provides counseling, STI prevention, and community support. Contact: 044-43511459. An anchor organization for LGBTQ+ mental health in Tamil Nadu.

Eating disorder resources India — NIMHANS: NIMHANS Bengaluru has a dedicated eating disorder clinic with psychiatrists and dietitians experienced in anorexia, bulimia, and OSFED. This is one of the very few specialized eating disorder programs in India. OPD appointments: 080-46110007. For severe eating disorders, NIMHANS inpatient services are available.

Eating disorder resources — online community: The Reddit India community r/india and r/IndiaSocial occasionally have threads on eating and body image. More directly, the Instagram community around Indian body positivity (accounts like @bodypositiveindia) provides peer support. For structured support, iCall counselors can address eating disorder distress. Formal eating disorder support groups as a structured program are still sparse in India.

OCD-specific resources India — ERP therapy centers: Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) is the gold-standard treatment for OCD. NIMHANS Bengaluru has trained OCD specialists. A few private centers in Mumbai, Delhi, and Bengaluru offer structured ERP programs. The OCD India forum (ocdindia.com) provides peer support, therapist directories, and psychoeducation. OCD Foundation India is an emerging advocacy organization.

Trauma and PTSD resources — SAMVAD: SAMVAD is a counseling center associated with NIMHANS that provides trauma-informed therapy and community mental health support. For survivors of sexual assault, iCall and One Stop Centres (Sakhi Centres) — government-mandated facilities in each district — provide integrated medical, legal, and psychological help. One Stop Centre helpline: 181.

Rape and sexual assault crisis support: One Stop Centres (Sakhi Centres) are government-mandated facilities available in every district. Services include: medical examination, police liaison, legal aid, and psychological counseling — all under one roof, free. Women's helpline: 181. iCall also provides specialized support for sexual assault survivors. Snehi and Vandrevala are additional options.

Student mental health — IIT counseling contacts: Most IITs have a Student Wellness Center (SWC) or counseling service. IIT Bombay: Student Wellness Center (022-25767531). IIT Delhi: Counselling Service (011-26591999). IIT Madras: Student Wellness Centre (044-22578200). IIT Kharagpur: Counselling Services available via campus health center. Students should contact their institute's student affairs office if wellness center is not easily findable.

Student mental health — AICTE mandate: AICTE (All India Council for Technical Education) mandates that all affiliated engineering colleges appoint trained counselors. However, implementation is uneven. If your college counselor is unavailable or inadequate, iCall (9152987821) and YourDOST campus programs provide external alternatives. Students also have the right to request mental health accommodations through their institution.

Student mental health — YourDOST peer program: YourDOST partners with 250+ universities to embed peer counselors — trained student volunteers who provide first-level emotional support and referrals. The platform's campus version is often free for students at partner institutions. This lowers the barrier significantly for students who won't seek formal counseling but will talk to a peer.

Affordable therapy options — NGO counseling: Several NGOs in India offer free or sliding-scale counseling: iCall (TISS, free), Vandrevala Foundation (free helpline, subsidized therapy), Sangath (Goa-based, also operates digital mental health programs), and Parivarthan (Bengaluru, ₹200-500 sliding scale). These are significantly more accessible than private practice rates of ₹2,000-5,000/session.

Affordable therapy options — government psychiatric hospitals: Government psychiatric hospitals (like NIMHANS, IHBAS Delhi, LGB Regional Institute Assam) offer outpatient psychiatric and psychological services at minimal or no cost. Medications under the National Mental Health Programme are available free at district hospitals. These resources are underused due to stigma and poor awareness.

Sliding scale therapy in India: Some private therapists offer sliding scale fees — adjusting their rate based on client income. To find these therapists: ask directly when inquiring ('Do you offer a sliding scale or reduced rate?'), check iCall's therapist network, or look on platforms like Therapize India and The Heal Foundation which list affordable therapists.

Men's mental health — why men don't seek help: Research consistently shows Indian men underutilize mental health services. Key barriers: cultural masculinity norms ('mard rote nahi'), belief that therapy is for 'weak' people, lack of male role models who discuss mental health, and presenting symptoms (irritability, substance use, anger) not recognized as mental health issues. Vandrevala specifically has outreach programs targeting men.

Men's mental health — how to encourage a male friend: Direct conversations work better than hints. Say: 'Yaar, tu bahut mushkil mein lag raha hai. Main judge nahi kar raha — ek baar kisi se baat kar ke dekh.' Normalize by sharing: 'Maine khud therapy try ki thi.' Offer specific help: 'Main pehle session mein chalna chahoon toh bata.' Remove logistical barriers — look up a counselor for them, offer to go together.

Grief support groups India: Online grief support communities include iCall's grief counseling (email-based), and Facebook groups like 'Grief Support India.' For child loss, PETALS India provides peer support. Sarpanch (a grief support NGO) runs support groups in Mumbai. Most grief support in India is informal — religious rituals, community gatherings — but formal support groups are emerging in metro cities.

Substance use resources — NIMHANS de-addiction: NIMHANS Bengaluru has a dedicated Centre for Addiction Medicine offering inpatient and outpatient de-addiction services. Services include medical detox, counseling, and relapse prevention. Contact: 080-46110007. This is one of India's premier de-addiction facilities. Many government hospitals across states also have de-addiction wards under NMHP.

Substance use resources — AA India meetings: Alcoholics Anonymous India (aaindia.org) has chapters in most major cities. Meetings are free, anonymous, and peer-led. NA (Narcotics Anonymous) India also has widespread meetings. For online meetings, SMART Recovery India offers a science-based alternative to 12-step programs. iCall (9152987821) also provides counseling for substance-related distress.

Caregiver support — SCARF: Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF), based in Chennai, provides specialized services for families of people with serious mental illness — schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, severe depression. Services include family therapy, caregiver training, residential rehabilitation, and vocational support. Contact: 044-26460657. SCARF also has an excellent library of caregiver psychoeducation materials in Tamil, Hindi, and English.

Caregiver burnout resources: Family members caring for a person with serious mental illness experience significant secondary stress — often called caregiver burnout. Symptoms: exhaustion, resentment, depression, social isolation. Resources: SCARF (Chennai), iCall for caregiver distress, NIMHANS family intervention programs, and online communities like 'Supporting a Loved One with Mental Illness India' on Facebook.

Rural and remote access — iCall phone counseling: For people in rural or semi-urban India without reliable internet, iCall's phone line (9152987821) remains the most accessible formal mental health resource. Available Mon-Sat 8am-10pm. No smartphone required. Counselors are trained to work in audio-only format and are sensitive to rural and agricultural stressors including debt, crop failure, and caste-based discrimination.

Rural and remote access — Tele-MANAS: The government's Tele-MANAS program (14416) was specifically designed for rural reach. It operates in 20+ languages, is toll-free, and connects callers to NIMHANS and AIIMS-linked psychiatrists for complex cases. By 2024, Tele-MANAS had cells in all states and UTs, with a target of reaching primary health center populations through ASHA and ANM health workers.

Parivarthan Counseling — Bengaluru: Parivarthan offers affordable individual and couples counseling in Bengaluru on a sliding scale (₹200-500 per session). Also offers training programs for counselors. One of the rare organizations making professional therapy accessible to working-class clients in a metro. Contact via their website parivarthan.org.

Sangath — digital mental health programs: Sangath (Goa-based, national impact) has developed evidence-based digital mental health programs including EMPOWER (for depression) and programs for alcohol use, delivered via community health workers. Partners with government health systems. Research-driven and published in The Lancet. A model for how mental health can be scaled in India using lay counselors.

Online therapy comparison — choosing a platform: For free support: iCall or Tele-MANAS. For affordable Hindi support: Lissun. For app-based self-help: Wysa or InnerHour. For campus students: YourDOST. For corporate employees: MindPeers (if employer-partnered). For professional therapy at mid-price: Intellecte or YourDOST. For specialized LGBTQ+ support: iCall or Humsafar Trust. No single platform fits all — needs, budget, and language matter.

Finding a therapist checklist: Verify their credentials (RCI-registered psychologist, or psychiatrist with MD/DPM). Ask about their therapeutic approach — CBT, DBT, psychodynamic? Ask if they have experience with your specific concern. Ask about fees and cancellation policy. Assess comfort after first session — therapeutic alliance (how much you trust your therapist) predicts outcome more than any technique.

iCall LGBTQ+ affirming counseling — specifics: iCall publishes explicit statements that its counselors will not engage in conversion therapy or pathologize LGBTQ+ identities. They have provided training to counselors on queer-affirmative practice, gender dysphoria support, and navigating family rejection. LGBTQ+ callers can request a counselor specifically trained in queer issues.

Counseling for farmers and agrarian distress: India's agrarian crisis — debt, crop failure, climate instability — is a documented driver of suicide in farming communities. iCall has specific outreach programs in Maharashtra's rural districts. Vandrevala Foundation also reaches farm communities. NGO Mann Deshi in Satara runs mental health programs for rural women. The distress is systemic — counselors working in this space must also connect people to government debt relief schemes.

NIMHANS outpatient services — how to access: NIMHANS (Bengaluru) OPD is open Monday to Saturday, 9am-12pm for new cases. No referral letter needed for most OPD services. Registration is minimal cost (under ₹100). After initial assessment, follow-up appointments and medications are heavily subsidized. For people outside Bengaluru, NIMHANS tele-psychiatry services are available via appointment.

Disability-inclusive mental health resources: People with physical disabilities face higher rates of depression and anxiety but lower access to mental health services. iCall and Tele-MANAS can be accessed without mobility. For deaf users, iCall offers text-based counseling via email. Sangath's programs have been adapted for low-literacy populations. There is no comprehensive national mental health resource specifically for people with disabilities yet — a significant gap.

Substance use — iCall for dual diagnosis: Many people struggling with alcohol or drug use also have underlying depression, anxiety, or trauma. iCall counselors are trained in dual diagnosis support — addressing mental health and substance use together rather than treating them as separate problems. This is important because treating addiction without addressing underlying mental health often leads to relapse.

Peer support programs in India: Peer support — trained individuals with lived experience of mental illness providing support to others — is an emerging model in India. The Banyan (Chennai) employs peer support workers. iCall has peer-support training initiatives. Vandrevala's volunteer model incorporates peer elements. Peer support is evidence-based, reduces stigma, and extends the reach of professional services.

Online therapy — insurance coverage in India: Star Health Insurance and a few others now cover mental health therapy under their policies, following the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 mandate. However, coverage is often limited to in-person sessions with psychiatrists. Most online therapy platforms are not yet covered. If you have health insurance, check with your provider specifically for mental health benefits — it's an evolving landscape.

The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 — key rights: Under this law, every Indian citizen has the right to access mental health care, the right to confidentiality, the right to make advance directives about treatment, the right not to be discriminated against on grounds of mental illness, and the right to free treatment at government facilities. Awareness of these rights helps clients advocate for themselves in healthcare settings.

iCall email counseling — for those who can't talk: Agar calling mushkil lagta hai — shayad family ke saath ghar mein ho, ya anxiety se phone pe baat nahi ho pa rahi — iCall offers email counseling at icall@tiss.edu. You write in about your situation, and a trained counselor responds within 1-2 working days. This is particularly helpful for those who process better in writing or need time to articulate their feelings.

Affordable psychiatry in India: Private psychiatrist appointments in metro cities cost ₹1,000-3,000. Government psychiatric OPDs are almost free (₹50-200) but have long queues. NIMHANS, IHBAS Delhi, CIP Ranchi, and LGB Regional Institute Assam offer subsidized care. Some NGO-linked psychiatrists (via Vandrevala Foundation) offer reduced-fee consultations. Medications under Jan Aushadhi Scheme are available at 50-90% discount at government centers.

Postpartum mental health resources India: Postpartum depression affects roughly 1 in 5 new mothers in India, yet is heavily underdiagnosed — often dismissed as 'adjustment to motherhood.' iCall provides counseling for new mothers. Fortis and Apollo hospital chains have psychiatrists experienced in perinatal mental health. Online communities like 'Moms of India' on Facebook offer peer support. Fathers can also experience postpartum depression and should be screened. Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is the standard screening tool.
